title: Skills
response()
text:
Render a Chameleon template directly to a flask.Response.


Usage
Source


response(
    template_file, content_type="text/html", status_code=200, **template_data
)


The @template decorator is the comfortable path, but it cannot reach everywhere. Error handlers are registered with Flask directly, a view may need to render a different template down one branch, and a helper may build a response for a view to return. All of them have the same need: a template, a model, and a finished response. This function meets that need in one call.


Parameters


template_file: str

The Chameleon template file (path relative to the template folder).

content_type: str = "text/html"

The content type of the response (defaults to text/html).

status_code: int = 200

The HTTP status code of the response (defaults to 200).

**template_data: Any

Values passed to the template as the model.





Returns


 flask.Response

The rendered flask.Response.





Raises


 FlaskChameleonException

If global_init() has not been called yet.





Examples
@app.errorhandler(500)
def server_error(e):
    return chameleon_flask.response('errors/500.pt', status_code=500)

title: API Reference
text:
Everything the package exports, in the order you meet it: set the engine up once, decorate your views, render directly when the decorator cannot reach, and the two exceptions that tie it together.


Configuration

Point the engine at your templates folder once at app startup, and reset it when a test suite needs a clean slate.


global_init()

Initialize the Chameleon template engine.

engine.clear()

Reset the template engine to its uninitialized state.




Decorating views

The decorator that turns a view returning a dict into a rendered response, sync or async, and the one call that swaps the page for a friendly 404.


template()

Decorate a Flask or Quart view method to render a Chameleon template.

not_found()

Abort the current view and render a friendly 404 page.




Direct rendering

For error handlers, conditional branches, and anywhere else the decorator cannot reach: a template straight to a Response, or straight to an HTML string.


response()

Render a Chameleon template directly to a flask.Response.

engine.render()

Render a Chameleon template to an HTML string.




Exceptions

The base error for everything the engine raises on purpose, and the not-found signal that not_found() raises and @template catches. Importable from chameleon_flask directly or from chameleon_flask.exceptions.


FlaskChameleonException

Base exception for all chameleon-flask errors.

FlaskChameleonNotFoundException

Raised by not_found() to signal that a view should render a 404 page.

title: engine.render()
text:
Render a Chameleon template to an HTML string.


Usage
Source


engine.render(template_file, **template_data)


This is the bottom rung of the ladder: a model goes in, HTML comes out, and nothing is wrapped in a response. Reach for it when you want the markup itself, for example to build an email body or to tuck rendered HTML into a JSON payload. Decorated views and response() both end up here.


Parameters


template_file: str

The Chameleon template file (path relative to the template folder).

**template_data: Any

Values passed to the template as the model.





Returns


 str

The rendered HTML as a string.





Raises


 FlaskChameleonException

If global_init() has not been called yet, or if template_data contains the key encoding, which Chameleon reserves as a render argument and cannot expose to the template.

title: FlaskChameleonNotFoundException
text:
Raised by not_found() to signal that a view should render a 404 page.


Usage
Source


FlaskChameleonNotFoundException(
    message=None, four04template_file="errors/404.pt"
)


You will rarely raise or catch this yourself. not_found() raises it from deep inside a view, the @template decorator catches it on the way out and renders its template_file with an empty model and status code 404. It only escapes if the view is not decorated, which is the one situation where you might want to catch it.


Parameters


message: str | None = None

Optional description of the missing resource.

four04template_file: str = "errors/404.pt"

The template to render for the 404 response.





Attributes


message: str | None

The message passed in, if any.

template_file: str

The template the decorator will render for the 404 response.

title: chameleon-flask
section: The whole library in one view

title: chameleon-flask
text:
Installation
pip install chameleon_flask
Or uv add chameleon-flask. Python 3.10 or newer. The only runtime dependencies are flask[async] and Chameleon, and the [async] extra is what lets Flask run the async views shown below.

title: chameleon-flask
text:
Setting up
Create a folder in your web app to hold the templates. Any layout works; this one groups templates by the view module that renders them, which pays off later with default template names:
├── app.py
├── views.py
│
├── templates
│   ├── home
│   │   └── index.pt
│   └── shared
│       └── layout.pt

At app startup, tell the library where that folder is:
from pathlib import Path
import chameleon_flask

dev_mode = True

BASE_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
template_folder = str(BASE_DIR / 'templates')
chameleon_flask.global_init(template_folder, auto_reload=dev_mode)
global_init() builds one Chameleon template loader for the whole process. Do this once, before you define your views. The call is deliberately one-shot: a second global_init() buried in some module is ignored rather than swapping your template folder out from under you (pass cache_init=False if you really do mean it).
auto_reload deserves its own sentence. With it on, Chameleon re-reads a template whenever its file changes, which is exactly what you want while you are editing templates and exactly what you don’t want in production, where the compiled templates should stay cached. Tie it to your dev-mode flag and forget about it.

text:
Alpine.js, Vue, and friends
Chameleon is strict about attributes by default: anything outside its own TAL/METAL/i18n namespaces is rejected. That strictness collides head-on with attribute-based JavaScript frameworks, whose whole idiom is shorthand attributes like @click, :class, and x-data. Pass restricted_namespace=False and Chameleon lets them through unchanged:
chameleon_flask.global_init(
    template_folder,
    auto_reload=dev_mode,
    restricted_namespace=False,  # Enable Alpine.js / Vue-style attributes
)

title: chameleon-flask
chameleon-flask
text:
The small print
A few things are worth knowing before they find you:

Decorator order matters. Put the route decorator outermost and @template directly above the function. The route has to register the wrapper that produces a Response, not the raw view that returns a dict.
Names are resolved at decoration time. The bare @template form looks up its template file when your module is imported. If global_init() hasn’t run yet, it assumes a folder named templates relative to the working directory.
An async view behind another decorator. If you stack your own sync decorator between @template and an async def, make it use functools.wraps; the library looks through wraps chains to find the coroutine function. Without it, you get a clear error telling you to move @template next to the async def, rather than a silently un-awaited coroutine.
encoding is a reserved key. Chameleon takes it as a render argument, so a model containing encoding is rejected with a clear FlaskChameleonException instead of a confusing traceback. Rename the key.
It’s content_type, not mimetype. The decorator keyword was renamed in an earlier release.

title: chameleon-flask
text:
An example
example/example_app.py is a small, runnable Flask app that exercises everything on this page: a sync view, an async view, an XML response with a 201 status, and a catalog where item 99 does not exist and shows the friendly 404. Run it with python example/example_app.py and visit http://127.0.0.1:5555.
Coding agents can load the agent skill or read llms-full.txt, which also cover Chameleon’s TAL syntax and METAL layouts.

title: Changelog
text:
New Feature: Namespace Restriction Control
Added support for controlling Chameleon’s namespace restriction, enabling better compatibility with attribute-based JavaScript frameworks like Vue.js and Alpine.js.

What’s New
The global_init() function now accepts a restricted_namespace parameter (defaults to True for backward compatibility). When set to False, Chameleon only treats its own namespaces (TAL, METAL, i18n) specially, allowing all other attributes to pass through unchanged.


Usage
import chameleon_flask

# Turn off namespace restriction for Alpine.js/Vue.js compatibility
chameleon_flask.global_init(
    template_folder='templates',
    auto_reload=True,
    restricted_namespace=False  # <-- Enable attribute-based JS frameworks
)


Why This Matters
With restricted_namespace=False: - Chameleon only processes its own namespaces (tal:, metal:, i18n:) - All other attributes like x-data, x-on:click, x-bind:class, [@click](https://github.com/click), :class are left untouched - Perfect for templates using Alpine.js, Vue.js, or other attribute-based frameworks - No need to escape or work around Chameleon’s namespace restrictions


Backward Compatibility
This change is fully backward compatible. The default value is True, maintaining the existing behavior unless explicitly changed.

title: FlaskChameleonException
text:
Base exception for all chameleon-flask errors.


Usage
Source


FlaskChameleonException()


Catch this to handle anything the library raises on purpose, from a missing global_init() call to a view that returned something other than a dict or a Response. The message always says what went wrong and, where there is one, the fix.

title: engine.clear()
text:
Reset the template engine to its uninitialized state.


Usage
Source


engine.clear()


Forgets the cached template loader and the template folder, so the next global_init() call starts from scratch with whatever settings it is given. An app will rarely need this; it exists for test suites that initialize the engine against different template folders and must not leak state from one test into the next.

title: global_init()
text:
Initialize the Chameleon template engine.


Usage
Source


global_init(
    template_folder,
    auto_reload=False,
    cache_init=True,
    restricted_namespace=True
)


Point the library at your templates folder once, at app startup, and every decorated view in the process knows where to look from then on. Under the hood this creates a single Chameleon PageTemplateLoader, which compiles each template to Python bytecode the first time it renders and caches the result.
The call is one-shot by design. With cache_init=True (the default), later calls are silently ignored once the engine is initialized, so a stray second global_init() deep in some module cannot swap your template folder out from under you. To re-initialize with different settings, pass cache_init=False or call chameleon_flask.engine.clear() first.
Call this before any decorated view is defined: the bare @template form resolves its template file name at decoration time and relies on the folder recorded here.


Parameters


template_folder: str

Path to the template directory.

auto_reload: bool = False

Re-read a template whenever its file changes. Exactly what you want while editing templates and an unneeded file check per render in production, so tie it to your dev-mode flag.

cache_init: bool = True

If True, do nothing when the engine is already initialized.

restricted_namespace: bool = True

If True, only TAL/METAL/i18n namespaced attributes are allowed in templates. Set it to False to let attribute-based JavaScript frameworks such as Alpine.js and Vue use their shorthand (@click, :class, x-data).





Raises


 FlaskChameleonException

If template_folder is empty or is not a directory.





Examples
from pathlib import Path
import chameleon_flask

dev_mode = True
folder = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / 'templates'
chameleon_flask.global_init(str(folder), auto_reload=dev_mode)

title: not_found()
text:
Abort the current view and render a friendly 404 page.


Usage
Source


not_found(four04template_file="errors/404.pt")


Somewhere in most views there is a lookup that can come up empty: an item id that was deleted last week, a slug that never existed. Call this at that point, inside a view decorated with @template, and stop worrying about the rest of the function. It raises FlaskChameleonNotFoundException, the decorator catches it, and the visitor gets your 404 template in the site’s own look instead of the framework’s bare error text.
The 404 page is rendered with an empty model, text/html content type, and status code 404; the view’s own content_type and status_code do not apply to this path.


Parameters


four04template_file: str = "errors/404.pt"

The template to render for the 404 response. Defaults to errors/404.pt; an empty or blank value falls back to that same default.





Raises


 FlaskChameleonNotFoundException

Always; the @template decorator turns it into the rendered 404 response.





Examples
@app.get('/catalog/item/<int:item_id>')
@chameleon_flask.template('catalog/item.pt')
def item(item_id: int):
    item = service.get_item_by_id(item_id)
    if not item:
        chameleon_flask.not_found()

    return {'item': item}

title: template()
text:
Decorate a Flask or Quart view method to render a Chameleon template.


Usage
Source


template(template_file=None, content_type="text/html", status_code=200)


This is the decorator the library is built around. The view underneath it returns a plain dict, and the decorator renders that dict through the template into a finished flask.Response. Return a Flask/Quart Response instead (a redirect, say) and it is passed through untouched; the template never runs. Anything else raises FlaskChameleonException naming the offending type.
It works on sync and async views alike, bare (@template) or with arguments (@template('home/index.pt')). When used bare, the template file is derived from the view as {module}/{function_name}.html, falling back to .pt when no .html file exists in the template folder.
Two things are decided once, when the view is decorated, not per request. The first is the template file name: when relying on the bare form, call global_init() before defining your views, otherwise the .html-or-.pt check assumes a folder named templates relative to the working directory. The second is whether the view is async. A sync decorator stacked between @template and an async def is handled as long as it uses functools.wraps; without it the view’s coroutine cannot be awaited and a clear error is raised, so place @template closest to the async def in that case.
Put the route decorator outermost and @template directly above the function. The route must register the wrapper that produces a Response, not the raw view.


Parameters


template_file: Callable[…, Any] | str | None = None

Optional, the Chameleon template file (path relative to the template folder, e.g. home/index.pt). Derived from the view when omitted.

content_type: str = "text/html"

The content type of the response (defaults to text/html).

status_code: int = 200

Default status code for responses. For example 201 on a POST/create action.





Returns


 Callable[…, Any]

The decorator to be consumed by Flask or Quart.





Raises


 FlaskChameleonException

At request time, if the view returns anything other than a dict or a recognized Response object, or if global_init() was never called.





Examples
@app.get('/')
@chameleon_flask.template('home/index.pt')
def index():
    return {'message': 'Hello world'}


@app.get('/listing')
@chameleon_flask.template  # Bare: renders {module}/{function_name}.html or .pt
async def listing():
    return {'items': await db.all_items()}
